# 68% of Americans Are Excited for Pumpkin Spice Season, but Consumers Pay Up to 75% More for Products


Written by


[Maggie Gunara](https://www.lendingtree.com/writer/maggie-gunara/)


Edited by


[Dan Shepard](https://www.lendingtree.com/writer/dan-shepard/)


Updated Oct 05, 2026


We are committed to providing accurate content that helps you make informed money decisions. Our partners have not commissioned or endorsed this content. Read oureditorial guidelines here .


Fall officially means one thing for retailers: pumpkin everything. This year, shoppers are showing up for it, even though pumpkin-flavored products carry a noticeably higher price tag than their standard counterparts.


Our research shows that while enthusiasm for pumpkin spice is nearing a five-year high, the premiums attached to it are also rising. Yet many consumers say they’re not willing to pay whatever it costs to get their seasonal fix.


Key takeaways


- **Pumpkin products carry a higher price tag.** Pumpkin-flavored items cost 8.9% more on average in 2026 than their nonpumpkin counterparts, up slightly from the 8.4% premium in our 2025 analysis.
- **By retailer, Starbucks has the highest average premium.** Its pumpkin product comparisons average a 19.7% premium, with nine out of 10 items analyzed costing more than their nonpumpkin counterparts. Trader Joe’s averages 11.8%, while Target averages 8.4%.
- **By product, a Trader Joe’s cereal shows the largest individual markup.** Pumpkin O’s cost $3.49 for 12 ounces, or $0.29 per ounce, versus $1.99 for 12 ounces of Joe’s Os, or $0.17 per ounce. That’s a 75.4% premium. Jade Leaf’s organic pumpkin spice matcha latte mix at Target follows at 47.2% more per ounce than its organic matcha latte mix, while Target’s Favorite Day pumpkin spice whipped dairy topping costs 44.6% more per ounce than its original counterpart.
- **Pumpkin spice enthusiasm is up so far this year.** Search interest for pumpkin spice at the start of September was at its second-highest level in the past five years, according to Google Trends data. By state, West Virginia remains No. 1 for pumpkin spice enthusiasm, while Cheyenne, Wyo., takes the top spot among metros.
- **Consumers like pumpkin spice but are wary of the hype.** More than two-thirds (68%) of Americans are at least a little excited about its fall return, and 63% say they enjoy the flavor. Still, 57% believe pumpkin spice products are overmarketed.
- **Many shoppers resist paying extra.** Nearly half of consumers (48%) say they generally wouldn’t pay more for a pumpkin or pumpkin spice version of a product they already buy, while 36% would pay a premium. Only 21% expect to spend more on pumpkin spice this fall than they did last fall.


## Pumpkin spice comes with a price premium


On average, pumpkin-flavored products cost 8.9% more than their nonpumpkin versions in 2026, an uptick from the 8.4% premium measured in 2025. (LendingTree analyzed 100 pumpkin and nonpumpkin comparisons across six retailers — see themethodology for specifics.)


**Pumpkin-flavored premium over the years**


Year Premium


2026 8.9%


2025 8.4%


2024 7.4%


2022 14.1%


2020 8.8%


2017 8.0%


Source: LendingTree analyses.


While that’s a seemingly modest number, Matt Schulz — LendingTree chief consumer finance analyst and author of “Ask Questions, Save Money, Make More: How to Take Control of Your Financial Life” — says the extra expense can pile up for anyone buying pumpkin-flavored products regularly.


“No one pumpkin purchase is likely to wreck your budget, but the trouble comes when you’re paying extra for multiple things week after week,” he says. “These purchases should be part of your fun-money budget, not something that gets a free pass because it’s temporary.”


## Starbucks has the highest average premium


Getting your fall-flavored caffeine fix may cost you more at Starbucks. Across the six retailers analyzed — Dunkin’, Foodtown, Starbucks, Target, Trader Joe’s and Whole Foods — Starbucks had the highest average premium, at 19.7%. There, nine of the 10 items analyzed cost more than their nonpumpkin counterparts.


Trader Joe’s followed, averaging an 11.8% premium, while Target’s pumpkin products averaged an 8.4% premium. Meanwhile, Dunkin’ had a 2.0% premium, Whole Foods had a 0.7% premium, and Foodtown had no markup (though we analyzed only one set of items there).


## One cereal has a 75.4% markup


Zooming in on individual products, Trader Joe’s Pumpkin O’s cost $3.49 for 12 ounces, or $0.29 per ounce. That compares with $1.99 for the same size of Joe’s Os cereal, or $0.17 per ounce. That works out to a 75.4% premium for the pumpkin version — the steepest markup among the 100 product comparisons analyzed.


Other standouts include Jade Leaf’s organic pumpkin spice matcha latte mix at Target, which costs 47.2% more per ounce than its plain counterpart, and Target’s Favorite Day pumpkin spice whipped dairy topping, priced 44.6% higher per ounce than its original counterpart.


Three of the five products with the biggest pumpkin spice markups are at Trader Joe’s, while the remaining two are at Target.


Schulz says a markup like that doesn’t have to mean giving up a favorite seasonal treat entirely.


“You don’t have to give up your favorite guilty pleasure; you just need to be thoughtful and planful about it,” he says. “Buy it once or twice instead of every week. Get a small or medium instead of a large. Skip another favorite of yours for a little while to make room for it in your budget. The goal is to find a way to enjoy the things you value most without letting them take away from bigger priorities.”


But not every pumpkin spice product comes with a premium. Of the 100 product comparisons, 55 have markups, 32 have no price difference and 13 cost less than their plain counterparts. Target’s Harney & Sons pumpkin spice herbal tea sachets have the biggest discount, costing 30.3% less than the brand’s raspberry herbal tea sachet counterpart. Next are Whole Foods’ NuttZo pumpkin spice power fuel 7-nut-and-seed butter (21.5% less) and Target’s Coffee mate pumpkin spice creamer (20.0% less). (See the full rankings below for the specific comparisons.)

## Interest in pumpkin spice is climbing even as prices rise


Higher prices don’t seem to be dampening interest. Google search interest in pumpkin spice is at its second-highest level in the past five years (Sept. 1, 2021, through Sept. 1, 2026), according to Google Trends data. The highest level was recorded during the week of Sept. 1, 2023. (That week, Dunkin’ Rewards members began receiving offers for a $3 pumpkin spice signature latte.)


As for why interest in pumpkin spice may be rising this year, Schulz points to the same forces that drive much seasonal spending.


“Seasonal products are built around urgency,” he says. “They’re only here for a short time, everyone seems to be talking about them and social media can make it feel as though you’re missing out if you don’t join in. There are few better examples of that than pumpkin spice. However, by making a shopping list and a budget that takes this seasonal spending into account, you can make it more likely that your passion for pumpkin won’t do real damage to your finances.”


By state, West Virginia remains No. 1 for relative pumpkin spice search interest — it also ranked first in last year’s analysis — followed by Maine and Pennsylvania. Mississippi, Louisiana and the District of Columbia have the lowest relative search interest.


Drilling down by metro, Cheyenne, Wyo., takes the top spot among the 209 metros analyzed, followed by Clarksburg, W.Va., and Presque Isle, Maine. All three metros with the lowest relative search interest are in Mississippi: Greenwood, Jackson and Meridian.

## Consumers enjoy pumpkin spice, but many think it’s oversold


Excitement for pumpkin spice season runs high. Among the 2,000 consumers surveyed, 68% are at least a little excited about the return of pumpkin spice products this fall.


Younger adults are especially excited, with 85% of Gen Zers ages 18 to 29 and 79% of millennials ages 30 to 45 saying they’re at least a little excited about the return of pumpkin spice products, compared with 62% of Gen Xers ages 46 to 61 and 47% of baby boomers ages 62 to 80.


Meanwhile, 63% of Americans say they enjoy the flavor. Despite that, 57% believe pumpkin spice products are overmarketed. Overall, though, 65% say pumpkin spice is a seasonal must-have at least sometimes.


So how can shoppers tell the difference between a planned indulgence and spending that’s being driven by advertising or fear of missing out? Schulz says the distinction might not matter, as long as spending is intentional.


“One of the simplest ways to do that is to have a ‘fun money’ or ‘entertainment’ line item in your budget,” he says. “Still, if you’re concerned about being too susceptible to advertising and feelings of FOMO, consider leveraging tools to help you combat those feelings. One of the most effective is the 24-hour rule. With it, you wait 24 hours before making any major purchase. If, after that time, you’re still compelled to buy the item, go for it. If you’re not, then skip it.”


## Many shoppers say they won’t pay just any price for the season


When it comes to opening their wallets, consumers are more cautious than the hype might suggest. Nearly half (48%) say they generally wouldn’t pay extra for a pumpkin or pumpkin spice version of a product they already buy, while 36% would pay a premium.


Just 21% expect to spend more on pumpkin spice this fall than they did last fall, while 32% expect to spend the same and 15% plan to spend less. Meanwhile, 27% didn’t buy any pumpkin spice products last year and don’t expect to this year, while 5% say they didn’t buy any last year but plan to buy pumpkin spice products this year.


Among those planning to buy pumpkin spice products this year, 41% agree that their love of pumpkin spice puts a strain on their budget, while 45% disagree and 14% say they don’t love pumpkin spice.


Schulz says there’s no magic formula for how much a seasonal upgrade is worth.


“The best move is to set your limit before you shop, either as a dollar amount for the season or a maximum amount you’re willing to pay over the regular product,” he says. “Whatever limit you choose, the extra should come from discretionary money. If it requires[carrying debt](https://www.lendingtree.com/debt-consolidation/) or shortchanging savings, it’s too expensive.”


## Managing a pumpkin spice budget: Top expert tips


All that sugar and spice isn’t so nice on the budget, but that doesn’t mean you can’t have your seasonal treats. To help account for the pumpkin spice premium in your budget, Schulz recommends:


- **Focus on unit prices.** “The overall price doesn’t always tell the whole story of how expensive something is,” Schulz says. “Make sure you pay attention to the per-unit price before you put the item in your cart.”
- **Set a firm**[budget](https://www.lendingtree.com/personal/budget-to-pay-off-debt/) **and track it.** “A well-made budget should be driven by the spending that matters to us most,” he says. “Being thoughtful about how much you’re willing to spend and then making sure you’re sticking within those boundaries can help ensure that you don’t impulse-buy yourself into trouble.”
- **Leverage credit card rewards.** “The right credit card, used wisely, can extend your budget,” he says. “An extra 1% or 2% cash back doesn’t sound like much, but it adds up over time, and that can create a little extra room for indulgences.”


## Methodology


LendingTree researchers gathered prices and sizes for 200 grocery store and coffee retailer products to estimate the average pumpkin spice premium. The sample included 100 pumpkin and 100 nonpumpkin products.


We compared the products by price per ounce (or price per item/count) to control for differences in size.


Our analysis involved a mix of online and in-store browsing from Sept. 1 to 8, 2026. We gathered data from the following grocery store and coffee retailers:


- Dunkin’
- Foodtown
- Starbucks
- Target
- Trader Joe’s
- Whole Foods


Because retailer prices vary across the country, we focused on prices in the following Brooklyn, N.Y., ZIP codes:


- 11201 (Trader Joe’s)
- 11216 (Dunkin’, Foodtown)
- 11217 (Target, Whole Foods, Starbucks)


Researchers also analyzed Google Trends data to determine when and where search interest in pumpkin spice is highest, covering all 50 states and the District of Columbia as well as the 209 largest metros.


Additionally, LendingTree commissioned QuestionPro to conduct an online survey of 2,000 U.S. consumers ages 18 to 80 from Sept. 2 to 6, 2026. The survey was administered using a nonprobability-based sample, and quotas were used to ensure the sample base represented the overall population. Researchers reviewed all responses for quality control.


We defined generations as the following ages in 2026:


- Generation Z: 18 to 29
- Millennial: 30 to 45
- Generation X: 46 to 61
- Baby boomer: 62 to 80

**Home Equity Loans** generally provide borrowers with a lump-sum loan amount secured by the equity in their home and typically feature a fixed interest rate and consistent monthly payments over the repayment term. Interest paid on a Home Equity Loan may be tax deductible; however, consumers should consult with a financial advisor or tax professional regarding their individual circumstances. Consumers should also ask lenders about any applicable prepayment penalties.


**Home Equity Lines of Credit (HELOC)** are revolving lines of credit secured by the equity in your home that allow borrowers to access funds during a defined draw period, such as 10 years. During the draw period, borrowers may draw funds as needed, repay amounts owed, and draw additional funds again, similar to the use of a credit card. HELOCs may be a suitable option for borrowers who do not need all available funds at one time. HELOCs generally have variable interest rates tied to a predefined index, such as the U.S. Prime Rate, which means monthly payment amounts may fluctuate over time. Repayment terms vary by lender and may include both a draw period and a repayment period, such as a 30-year term that includes a 10-year draw period.
